terms.comment: From assideō: first of a person always there, sitting at a task (a constant companion, a farmer always on his land), then of things that never let up, storms, rain, work. Constantly: assiduē (Lewis & Short).
Unbroken from end to end (see permanent). Constantly: perpetuō.
Of days, nights and years, following one after another without a break: continuōs complūrēs diēs, several days running. Of place, joined on, unbroken (Lewis & Short).
Literally “go with me”. We have found no ancient source for it in Lewis & Short or the loci collections.

phrases.latin: num istīc quoque immīte et turbidum caelum? hīc assiduae tempestātēs et crēbra dīluvia
phrases.english: is the sky wild and stormy where you are too? Here it is constant storms and one flood after another

phrases.latin: cūnārum fuerās mōtor, Charidēme, meārum et puerī custōs assiduusque comes
phrases.english: you rocked my cradle, Charidemus, and were my guardian as a boy and my constant companion

phrases.latin: Secūtae sunt continuōs complūrēs diēs tempestātēs, quae et nostrōs in castrīs continērent et hostem ā pugnā prohibērent.
phrases.english: There followed several days of storms without a break, which kept our men in camp and the enemy from fighting.

sources: Lewis & Short: assiduus · Lewis & Short: perpetuus · Lewis & Short: continuus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 296.
